podcast.title: Launch and Impact on Industry (2008)
podcast.body: Spotify went online in 2008, a year that saw drastic changes in the recorded music industry due to music piracy and freefalling CD sales. This streaming platform promised "unlimited access to music for free or something very close to it," contributing to the drying up of money for big spending on marketing and promotion, including music video budgets. "By the time we arrived in 2008, the year Spotify went online, the recorded music industry had changed drastically."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Rise and Fall and Future of the Music Video - Part 2

podcast.title: Daniel Ek's 2020 Statement on Artist Viability
podcast.body: In 2020, Spotify CEO Daniel Ek commented on the evolving music landscape, stating that artists who previously succeeded by releasing music every few years might not thrive in the streaming era, implying a need for more frequent output. "Spotify CEO Daniel Eck had this to say in 2020. Some artists that used to do well in the past may not do well in this future landscape, where you can't record music once every three to four years and think that that's going to be enough."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: 23 Points About Streaming: Part 2

podcast.title: Artist Payment Model – Percentage Share
podcast.body: Spotify's payment model for artists is based on their overall percentage share of total streams; if an artist like Justin Bieber accounts for 'X' percent of streams in a month, they receive the same 'X' percentage of the total revenue. "The way it works is that Spotify pays artists on their overall percentage share."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: 23 Points About Streaming: Part 2

podcast.title: Dominance and Skip Data
podcast.body: Spotify became a dominant force in music streaming, providing access to over 110 million songs by the mid-2010s. In 2016, data revealed that 24% of its listeners skip a song in the first 5 seconds if they don't like it, 29% skip within 10 seconds, and 34% are gone by 30 seconds, indicating shortened attention spans. "In 2016, it was revealed that 24% of Spotify listeners will skip a song in the first 5 seconds if they don't recognize it or decide they don't like it."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The History of the 2010s Part 1: Rock Struggles Again

podcast.title: Founding and Global Rollout
podcast.body: Spotify was founded in 2006 and began its online rollout country by country in 2008. It launched in the US in July 2011 and in Canada in 2014, becoming a major player in the global streaming music market. "Spotify was founded in 2006 and began going online country by country in 2008."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The History of the 2010s Part 1: Rock Struggles Again

podcast.title: Influence on Song Composition
podcast.body: The platform's payment structure, which only compensates artists after a song runs for at least 30 seconds, has influenced how music is composed. Artists now prioritize holding a listener's attention during this initial half-minute, leading to shorter intros, front-loaded choruses, and an abundance of "sugary hooks" in the first 30 seconds. "no one gets paid until a song runs for at least 30 seconds."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The 100 Greatest Rock Moments of the Millennium So Far - Part 10: (10-1)

podcast.title: Listener Behavior and "Lean Back Listening"
podcast.body: Streaming has altered music consumption habits, with many using music as background "soundtrack" to fill silence, rather than actively listening. This phenomenon, termed "lean back listening," involves passively letting music come to the listener by simply clicking play, contrasting with "lean forward music," which involves actively seeking out, absorbing, and appreciating music. This shift has impacted how algorithms work, the kind of music composers create, and general attitudes toward the abundant music supply. "We've created a situation where a lot of us are hearing music, but not listening."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The 100 Greatest Rock Moments of the Millennium So Far - Part 10: (10-1)

podcast.title: Low Payouts and Artist Compensation
podcast.body: Spotify, like other streaming platforms, offers significantly lower payouts to artists compared to traditional physical sales. While it provides global reach for a song, the revenue per stream is often equivalent to radio play. This economic model has led to a "thin layer of very successful artists on top" and millions of struggling artists at the bottom, forcing many to rely on alternative income streams like merchandise, touring, and licensing. "Streaming pays out much less than the sales of physical formats."

Volunteers listened to various playlists while engaging in non-verbal reasoning tests designed to lower stress, with their blood pressure monitored throughout. podcast.title: Skipping Behavior Data
podcast.body: Spotify usage data indicates a significant tendency for users to skip songs: 25% of users skip an unfamiliar new song within the first five seconds, another 29% skip within 10 seconds, and 35% are gone by the 30-second mark. This behavior contributes to the devaluation of music as both an art form and a commodity. "According to some Spotify numbers I saw while back, 25% of users will skip an unfamiliar new song in the first five seconds."

podcast.body: Spotify has become a dominant force in the streaming music industry, boasting 625 million monthly users and valuing the company at $125 billion, a figure greater than the entire recorded music industry combined. podcast.title: Untouched Music Library
podcast.body: It is estimated that 20% of the songs in Spotify's library, which contains over 110 million tracks, have never been streamed by anyone even once. This equates to more than 20 million unheard songs, raising questions about lost music and missed opportunities for discovery. "On Spotify alone, it's estimated that 20% of the songs in the library have not been streamed by anyone even once."

podcast.body: It is possible to load music onto an Apple Watch for swimming and listen using waterproof Bluetooth headphones.
